core_fields.title: Digital agriculture – Algeria (2023)
core_fields.description: As part of the WaPOR phase 2 project (GCP/INT/729/NET), supported by the FAO and funded by the Netherlands, Algeria has implemented a WAPOR digitization Cell  within the Ministry of Agriculture. This initiative aims to strengthen national capacities in monitoring land and water productivity thru remote sensing. The WaPOR cell  plays a central role in integrating satellite data to improve the management of agricultural water resources, optimize cultivation practices, and support data-driven decision-making. It is part of a regional strategy for the digital transformation of agriculture, with activities in training, technology transfer, and inter-institutional collaboration. Algeria, alongside countries like Tunisia, Morocco, and Egypt, benefits from technical support to adapt WaPOR tools to local realities and promote more sustainable and resilient agriculture.

core_fields.title: Digital agriculture – Antigua and Barbuda (2023)
core_fields.description: In Antigua and Barbuda, FAO introduced a precision agriculture innovation by providing farmers with portable environmental sensors capable of measuring soil pH, electrical conductivity (EC), moisture, and nutrient levels. These digital tools enable real-time analysis via mobile apps, helping farmers make informed decisions about fertilization and irrigation. A hands-on training workshop was conducted for 21 participants, including farmers and extension officers, to build capacity in using the technology. This initiative, part of the project TCP/SLC/3808, aims to enhance productivity, resilience, and sustainability in horticultural crop management, addressing challenges like land degradation, water variability, and nutrient depletion.

core_fields.title: Digital agriculture – Ethiopia (2023)
core_fields.description:
The Flexible Multiparter Mechanism (FVC) sub-programme within the Global Network on Digital Agriculture Innovation Hubs (FMM/GLO/159/MUL) is actively implemented in Ethiopia to advance the integration of digital agriculture innovations and foster the transformation of agri-food systems. The FAO office in Ethiopia has established the Digital Agriculture and Innovation Hub, aligning with Ethiopia's Digital 2025 strategy for Agriculture and Food Transformation. 
In the current implementation cycle, the hub prioritized supporting producers, value chain actors, and young women innovators. An Agri-innovation Bootcamp capacitated 80 youths on translating innovative ideas into scalable ventures, addressing challenges in agriculture and the agrifood system. Demand-driven innovation and rural entrepreneurship training for 35 youth farmers were conducted, promoting innovative solutions to enhance productivity. 
The Digital Agriculture and Innovation Hub launched a monthly webinar, serving as a platform for government representatives, private sectors, farmers, and development partners to discuss challenges and opportunities in the digital agriculture ecosystem. This initiative has influenced policy development and legislation to support the startup ecosystem in Ethiopia. 
The sub-program stimulated innovation by sharing knowledge and methods among innovators, farmers, and experts. It emphasized a unique learning approach, focusing on experience sharing among developing countries facing similar challenges, rather than solely relying on insights from developed nations.

Information on main beneficiaries of rep.value: Women and youth

Comments.value: SD-FVC with global network on digital agriculture innovation Hub for advancing the integration of digital agriculture innovations and foster the transformation of agri-food systems in Ethiopia. Digital agriculture innovation hub established is aligned with the country digital strategy for agric and food transformation.

core_fields.title: Digital agriculture – Nepal (2023)
core_fields.description:
FAO-Nepal piloted and implemented the Tele Plant Doctor. Powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and computer vision, this mobile application helps crop disease detection by allowing farmers and technicians to simply upload images of infected plant leaves for instant analysis and diagnosis. The app then analyzes these images, identifies disease symptoms and pests, and provides management recommendations in the local language. This approach helps reduce crop losses, promotes the judicious use of pesticides, and enhances food security and safety.

The app is a game-changer, especially given that diseases and pests account for approximately 40% of agricultural production losses globally. The Tele Plant Doctor not only detects these issues but also recommends eco-friendly management solutions, directly contributing to sustainable agrifood systems. It empowers farmers to make informed decisions and adopt best practices by providing accurate and timely information.

Supported by the FAO's Digital Village Initiative (DVI), this innovation leverages advanced AI, Machine Learning, and Computer Vision technologies. It empowers farmers by providing timely, accurate disease-pest identification and effective management recommendations, reducing reliance on traditional, resource-intensive plant protection services.

Currently used for crops like potatoes and tomatoes, the app detects diseases such as Potato Early Blight, Tomato Bacterial Leaf Spot, and many more. The success of this initiative has led to plans for expanding its capabilities, including identifying nutrient deficiencies and predicting disease occurrences based on geolocation-specific data.


Nepal's Minister for Agriculture and Livestock Development has highlighted the importance of the Tele Plant Doctor application, marking it as a significant step towards elevating agrifood systems in Nepal. This recognition underscores the app's potential to transform traditional agricultural practices and enhance the efficiency of crop management across the country.

Information on main beneficiaries of rep.value:
The applicaiton was launched by FAO DG at Kuntabesi Kavre where farmers are adopting IPM and grow mainly potatoes.
This mobile application can be directly used by farmers or agricultural technician to accurately detect the plant diseases.

core_fields.title: Other Area – Syrian Arab Republic (2023)
core_fields.description:
Innovative response to the impact of high fertilizers prices nationally and globally and promoting the adoption of organic farming practices.
Fertilizer prices have risen over the past several months (and years) in Syria due to high energy prices and reduced supply. The conflict in Europe has also reduced global supply of fertilizer, coupled with the economic challenges affecting Syria, which in turn affect the importation of some types of fertilizer.  
To circumvent the high fertilizer prices and limited supply and availability of imported fertilizers, FAO Syria incorporated the production of organic liquid fertilizer into the FFS curriculum as an alternative using their own resources This is being done to improve the resilience of vulnerable smallholder farmers to this specific shock, at the same time promoting organic production. The production of organic liquid fertilizer from cattle manure is a ,low cost and short term process, minimum work load mainly for women, simple, practical and easy to apply innovation. 
In 2023 FAO built the capacity of farmers to produce organic liquid fertilizer from cow manure and this improved the adoption of sustainable agricultural practices and reduced the reliance on synthetic inputs. Additionally, the organic fertilizer will help farmers to improve soil structure and fertility, soil microbial activity and promote overall soil health in the medium to long-term.

Information on main beneficiaries of rep.value: Male and female Farmer field school (FFS) participants, including those with disability.

Comments.value: (1 of the 5 examples selected for the GMR)
